pieces.title: Comets Have Feathers
pieces.observation: This game, where you fly as a dragon in a 3D world, reminded me so much of the old collect-a-thon days with Banjo Kazooie and Mario 64. It's not a collect-a-thon, but the freedom invited to go everywhere and the the lack of yellow-paint-hand-holding makes this one of my favorite games to just relax and feel the freedom.
pieces.intention: The developers built this game around the joy of flying and the satisfaction of chaining together ball-slam attacks, inspired by the sensation of piloting a helicopter made accessible and safe. They are experimenting with three specific design challenges: a single interconnected map inspired by Bowser's Fury, a unified health-and-ammo resource that creates meaningful consequences, and parry-dodge combat from the air that feels immediate and personal. The emotional arc builds from whimsy and curiosity in early exploration.
pieces.hint: the one where you fly in an open world

quiz.q: What did the developer do before working in games?
quiz.from: I used to fly Helicopters - I came to work in the game industry much later in life than most I think.

quiz.q: Who did the character animations?
quiz.from: My daughter is an animator, but has had trouble getting into the industry... she's done the animations for the characters.

quiz.q: What move did the whole game end up built around?
quiz.from: I think it all centered around the ball slam - once we started playing with that Idea, I really just started scrapping everything else in favor of using that as our 'jump'.

drinkLine: A mixture of blue berry syrup and lemonade with just enough caffeine to give you wings.
answers:
"Whimsy and Curiosity - Early on the game should feel somewhat Whimsical, and the player should feel curious about the world, with them wondering ""what's going to happen next?""

Exhilaration (maybe that's too strong a term? Joy maybe?) - at being able to fly anywhere

Surprise - Ball Slam should surprise the player early on - it's not what you would expect at first from a game like this.

There are other intended emotions later in the game - it hasn't been implemented yet, but there is a bit of a darker turn that occurs just before the 3rd act, and I'm hoping to elicit some anxiety from the player there. "

"My daughter is an animator, but has had trouble getting into the industry - so, we came up with something that we could work on together, at first as a portfolio piece, but I want to make sure that it's something that 'ships' so that there is a steam page she can send folks to see her work - she's done the animations for the characters.  Most of the characters are assets that we got off the various storefronts, but she's taken them, re-rigged them, and re-animated them.

I used to fly Helicopters - I came to work in the game industry much later in life than most I think - but I've never gotten the chance to work on any kind of flying game (there was flying in a previous game that I made called TO THE TOP - a VR game - but, it wasn't a central focus).  I wanted to try to make a game that reminded me a little of flying helicopters, but much more accessible, and somewhat less explodey.

By trade, I am a senior gameplay programmer, but there are a few design challenges that I'm attempting to take a crack at:
- Single Large Map (not sure that I'd call it open world exactly, but the game will take place in one map) - inspired by Bowsers Fury more than other open world games.

- The idea of 'Ammo is Health' - you burn your 'health' with most of your actions - what I wanted to try here was condensing all the bars you see in many games down to just one resource

- Flying - designing an adventrure-ish game with a character that can fly is tricky, and most designers tell me to just put the player in a box - restrict where the player can go (which, to be fair, is kind of how it is currently), but I like the idea that maybe you *can* make a game with a flying character that's fun and interesting and not just Crimson Skies.

- Parry/Dodge Combat from the air, but without just resorting to shooting at things - force the player to 'get in there' when they engage"

"I think it all centered around the ball slam - once we started playing with that Idea, I really just started scrapping everything else in favor of using that as our 'jump'.  I do feel that there is a bit of feeling of mastery that occurs once you figure out how to chain ball slams back to back and getting the timings down on parries.  The game feel there is unique, I think, and helps elicit that surprise.

The map itself helps with the curiosity - I think that it leads player to want to fly around and see what's behind that boulder, or in that forest of mushrooms - where does that vine pathway lead - that sort of thing.

Flying, and ball mode do seem to work well as 'cool factor' - however it doesn't last forever. I'm hoping that by mixing it up with the challenges - using the Baamadilloes, Enemy encounters, and simple puzzle-like activities (I really like the term coined by Vigil Games on Darksiders (RIP - long live Gunfire Games!) - ""Nuzzles""), that we can keep up that curiosity and 'what happens next' feeling for about 6 hours :P"
pieces.episodeTitle: The Game Design No One Can Talk About
pieces.cardBlurb: This collect-a-thon/non-collect-a-thon was strangely nostalgic. I completely got it.

pieces.title: Absorber
pieces.observation: Why does getting hurt in a tactics game feel so confusing when you can see the enemy right next to you? Absorber executes all actions simultaneously in a single frame, making it hard to parse who attacked whom and when. I spent hours learning that the red warning zones don't show attack range, that status effects are a history of what just happened rather than active buffs, and that enemies move in a hidden hierarchy. Yet beneath this opacity lies a surprisingly deep roguelike about building synergies between absorbed enemy abilities.
pieces.intention: Martin built Absorber around the conviction that every decision should have meaningful consequences. Inspired by 868-Hack, he wanted players to feel the tension of deciding whether to play it safe or push for growth, to think three moves ahead while barely hanging on. The core is absorbing weakened enemies to unlock their program-like abilities and combine them across runs, similar to Balatro's upgrade systems.
pieces.hint: the one where you absorb enemy powers

quiz.q: What did the developer want every decision to have?
quiz.from: I wanted the player to feel that every decision has consequences.

quiz.q: Which game had they wanted to make something like for a long time?
quiz.from: I'm a huge fan of 868 HACK, and I've wanted to make a game like it for a long time.

quiz.q: Which game's run-shaping upgrades did they point to?
quiz.from: ...build around them over time, similar to how Balatro lets you shape a run through upgrades.

answers: I wanted the player to feel that every decision has consequences.

I’m a huge fan of 868 HACK, and I’ve wanted to make a game like it for a long time. I especially love the idea of program like abilities, and in my game I want players to be able to buy them, unlock them, and build around them over time, similar to how Balatro lets you shape a run through upgrades.

I'm becoming something more powerful by embracing the system. Do I play it safe or push for growth?  I need to think three moves ahead. I'm barely hanging on, but I'm learning. I'm in the zone, everything is working. Every decision matters.

pieces.title: Hyperbaric
pieces.observation: Why does a game about guiding a glowing dot into a circle feel like cosmic horror? Hyperbaric strips away the visual noise that typically signals fear, and instead builds dread through pure interaction. As you struggle to keep a white dot centered in a green circle while an implicit timer counts down in your mind, the game shifts the difficulty in subtle ways. What emerges is the feeling of being one mistake away from disaster, with something massive and unseen waiting for you to slip.
pieces.intention: Made during the summer of 2020 while working as a delivery driver in pandemic Los Angeles, Hyperbaric channels the surreal of that experience: a solitary essential worker performing small, precise tasks with an ominous presence looming overhead, the constant awareness that one wrong move could be catastrophic.
pieces.hint: the one where you keep a creature sealed

quiz.q: What job was the producer doing while they made it?
quiz.from: This was made in summer of 2020 while I was driving for Door Dash full time, peak pandemic Los Angeles.

quiz.q: What is the monster chained to the ocean floor a metaphor for?
quiz.from: It's kind of a ham fisted metaphor, embodying COVID with some titanic monster chained to the ocean floor.

quiz.q: Which game's end-of-day timer did the programmer think of as a horror mechanic?
quiz.from: It was an era where i thought the pikmin end of day timer counting down while you try to beat the buzzer with one last piece was a horror mechanic.

answers:
"Kye (Producer and Sound Lead): This was made in summer of 2020 while I was driving for Door Dash full time, peak pandemic Los Angeles. Working such a mundane job during this time was surreal given how apocalyptic yet mundane it felt. I was just a dude delivering food in an almost completely empty city. I'd eat breakfast, launch the app, get into my car, deny some orders, accept an order to deliver a pizza, and then drive out into the city. A city of ten million where I'd see maybe a dozen people a day, and every single one of those interactions was haunted by COVID. It was super early pandemic so we still had no idea how bad COVID would get and it truly felt like this ominous presence looming over everything you did outside. As an essential worker it truly felt like I was forced to risk my life to make rent while this corporation cashed in off of it.

This was the vibe I really wanted us to nail for Hyperbaric. You play as a lone diver that lives in his relatively cozy diving bell only to be launched out into an abyss by an apathetic corporate entity. Yet despite it being empty you weren't alone. It's kind of a ham fisted metaphor, embodying COVID with some titanic monster chained to the ocean floor. Working a mundane job with little transparency where mistakes felt potentially lethal. While doing delivery driving the most risky times were when you were interacting with others, you never knew if you were about to make a mistake and get COVID. While diving you refresh the chained runes keeping the beast in place, one wrong step and it'll be unleashed upon you.

It sucked ass to live through and we wanted this game to suck ass to play (but in an intentional way.) A looming stress that you were never fully free from.

Elijah (Programmer): I was super hands off hyperbaric in (the design) respect, i was hyper focused on pretty much JUSt the welding minigame and making it feel as edge-of-the-knife as possible. I was really into the idea of the horror in a horror game coming from mechanics so i wanted to keep the player feeling like they were one flub away from fail state. It was an era where i thought the pikmin end of day timer counting down while you try to beat the buzzer with one last piece was a horror mechanic. Players were given a task that required full concentration while a timer ticked down and we added forces that made it harder to complete said task."

Honestly I feel I kinda answered this q in the last question but beyond my desire to embody the experience of being an essential worker during peak pandemic LA... beyond that it was just to pick a concept/setting where our artists could flex without us going out of scope for a 3 week jam.

Absolutely I think we did. People sweat bullets while playing but you don't die so often that the stress completely vanishes. Almost nobody picked up on the worker thing but that's okay, it wasn't about me it was about turning a unique personal experience into something others can experience.
pieces.episodeTitle: How Games Make Players Feel Small
pieces.cardBlurb: An incredible cosmic horror. But I missed the metaphor.

pieces.title: Club Soko
pieces.observation: Club Soko is charming and colorful, with a Sokoban puzzle core wrapped in nightclub aesthetics. But why does pushing drunk people around in this vibrant, absurd space feel so playful rather than critical? The developer hints at deeper meaning—anti-alcohol commentary, a graffiti artist navigating toward something darker—yet those messages seem to hide beneath the surface. Play it yourself and discover whether the game's satirical bite reveals itself to you, or whether its nightclub world remains simply fun to navigate.
pieces.intention: The developer wanted to create a love letter to Sokoban that also critiques how alcohol impacts people, similar to how The Binding of Isaac critiques religion. Mechanics serve as metaphor: you are a graffiti artist (representing creative pursuit) pushed around by nightclub patrons, progressing deeper into increasingly strange territory. The game uses subtle signals—character names referencing counterculture, hidden binary codes, punk aesthetics, dialogue hints—to invite players toward its message about choosing art over drinking.
pieces.hint: the one with the graffiti artist getting pushed around in the nightclub

quiz.q: What is Club Soko quietly commenting on?
quiz.right: The harm the alcohol industry can do
quiz.from: At a deeper level I wanted players who might be paying closer attention to pick up on the social commentary on how alcohol industry can have a negative impact on society.

quiz.q: Which game is it a love letter to?
quiz.from: The game is a bit of a love letter to The Binding of Isaac as that game is about how religion can have a negative impact on creative kids.

quiz.q: Who is the main character named after?
quiz.from: ...spraying hardcore punk motifs and her name Maude after the movie Harold & Maude as a symbol for counter culture.

answers:
"At a surface, I wanted the player to feel like they're navigating their way through rooms in a nightclub and going deeper into it.

At a deeper level I wanted players who might be paying closer attention to pick up on the social commentary on how alcohol industry can have a negative impact on society."

"I love the Sokoban subgenre, it was a throw back to my first ever game in 2012 made for GGJ which was also a Sokoban. I was itching to revisit a game subgenre I know and love.

The whole punk ethos embedded within and what the game is trying to communicate to the world excites me. I ultimately just want to make rad games that are trying to say something.
 
I had clear visuals of what the whole game will be from start to end which helped me make this game instead of another. Though I am working on multiple games at once, the creative process for making all the art and ideas in Club Soko poured out of me in a way that I didn't have to force."

"I believe there to be some mechanics as metaphor going on but I'll do my best to explain...

The game is a bit of a love letter to The Binding of Isaac as that game is about how religion can have a negative impact on creative kids. Club Soko is basically a game about how alcohol can have a negative impact on people.

You play as a graffiti artist that's spray painting the walls of the nightclub from the inside as you go deeper into it. It's intending to communicate to players that maybe the pursuit of making art is a healthier than the pursuit of drinking booze, I intentionally try to communicate that in a subtle way. The transition scenes show the player character sliding down a vent, spraying hardcore punk motifs and her name Maude after the movie Harold & Maude as a symbol for counter culture.

There's secret rooms and secret input codes and hidden binary and a acrostic in the late game to hint at its deeper meaning. We have an 'easy fun' dialogue system that's secondary to the core mechanics but exists to hint at the meaning of the game throughout progression. Bumping into other characters reveals more insight into this intended emotional response.

You can unlock cameo characters from other indie games like 'Twin Hobo Rocket' which is a nod to an early era Flash game with two drunk characters. All the names of puzzles on the back of the vinyl in the level select are references to real songs, many of which are associated with the hardcore punk movement or adjacent subcultures.

In Club Soko you're navigating around people that are drinking in nightclub rooms. You're essentially a black sheep that gets pushed around and only by the player thinking deeply and navigating around drunk people you're able to progress deeper.

I've learnt through making this game that good puzzles are something to do with making a context switch in the players mind. Club Soko attempts to entice a context switch towards a players own personal relationship with alcohol through solving it's puzzles."
pieces.episodeTitle: The Design Philosophy I Found Inside This Indie Game
pieces.cardBlurb: A really clever sokoban in a club atmosphere. The metaphor went over my head.

pieces.title: Sonak
pieces.observation: Sonak presents itself as an action game with combat that feels distant and abstract, but its real pull emerges slowly through systems and synergy. I found myself unexpectedly drawn into customizing a wizard character through meaningful item choices, discovering that attachment comes not from flashy animations but from watching a character become something I shaped.
pieces.intention: Sonak is built around giving players tools to express their playstyle through character building. The developers wanted players to feel weak at first, then gradually powerful as they acquire gear and levels—but they also wanted to support wildly different skill levels by letting players craft difficulty through their build choices. Whether someone wants a fast glass cannon or a slow tank that just absorbs damage, the game provides the systems to make it work.
pieces.hint: the one where you build your character through loot instead of combat

quiz.q: How should you feel at the start of the game?
quiz.right: Challenged: you're not strong enough yet
quiz.from: I want the player to feel challenge and struggle in the beginning of the game, as you are not strong enough to defeat the many enemies you encounter.

quiz.q: What kind of game is Sonak?
quiz.from: Sonak is a procedurally generated ARPG, which means beyond just the technical implementation challenges, there is also very complicated balance challenges.

quiz.q: Instead of hand-picking every drop, what does the developer give players?
quiz.right: Tools to build a character that fits their playstyle
quiz.from: I can give the players all of the tools I can, so that they can build the specific character that matches their playstyle.

answers: I want the player to feel challenge and struggle in the beginning of the game, as you are not strong enough to defeat the many enemies you encounter. But also excitement and joy as they find gear and gain levels that cause them to dramatically progress. You should feel a sense of attachment to your character as you define your build, and what strategy you will use to defeat the encounters. The longer you play your specific character, and the more items and levels you gain, I hope there is more attachment and wonder about the possible future for that character.

I like your extremely honest and direct approach to game reviews. I have watched many of your videos, and I like that you give your own personal experiences as an example of what things are done right, and what things can be improved. Right now I am in the stages of launching the demo for my game, and really would love as many eyes as possible on it. Both from a marketing perspective, but also from a design and confusion perspective so that I can produce the best possible game, and experience for my players.

Sonak is a procedurally generated ARPG, which means beyond just the technical implementation challenges, there is also very complicated balance challenges that I face as the developer. 

Some play testers are extremely skilled at fast action games, and understand how these sorts of games work from a crafting perspective, and thus completely dominate them. And others who are much less familiar, struggle with even the simplest combat experiences. 

So to come around to answering your question, my goals are to provide tools for the player to express their skill inside of the game however best fits their playstyle. I have provided all sorts of systems for tuning the difficulty both up and down, so that players can find the correct level, for that specific character that they are playing. 

I cant define specific items that drop, or even bosses they will encounter. But I can give the players all of the tools I can, so that they can build the specific character that matches their playstyle. From fast attacking glass cannon builds, to slow tanky hard hitting builds who can just stand still why being attacked.
pieces.episodeTitle: Why Do Some Games Feel More Real?
pieces.cardBlurb: Building a stat-based fighter is not my jam. But I ended up loving it.

pieces.title: Zeroth
pieces.observation: Zeroth presents a living world where termites eat wooden bows, monsters can be petrified and their eggs weaponized, and items interact in ways that create chaotic, surprising moments, but the game initially seems to demand that you discover these connections on your own, without guidance.
pieces.intention: Contrary Games built Zeroth to capture what they felt playing Hack and NetHack—roguelikes where every run tells a unique, emergent story through rich systems of verbs and interactions. They wanted to bring that essence to modern players with updated accessibility and animation. The game is built around procedural generation, permadeath, physics-based chaos, and systems where items meaningfully interact: materials matter, creatures have behaviors tied to their nature, and the world responds to your choices.
pieces.reaction: Thanks DeVaughn for all your time spent in Zeroth - your analysis helped me to understand that onboarding players is about WHY to play and not HOW to play. It's something that I'm still thinking about and it continues to challenge me as I work to complete Zeroth.
pieces.hint: the one where termites eat your wooden bow

quiz.q: What should make you laugh in Zeroth?
quiz.right: The avatar's reactions to what happens to it
quiz.from: We want the player to feel delight and amusement at the avatar's responses to what is happening to them.

quiz.q: Which classic game did the developers love?
quiz.from: We loved the experience of playing Nethack and other traditional roguelikes.

quiz.q: What is the game's core principle?
quiz.right: Every mechanic should interact with as many others as possible
wrong: Keep every system separate and simple
Always tell the player what an item does
quiz.from: The core principle of our game is that mechanics should all interplay with each other in as many ways as possible.

answers:
"We want the player to feel delight and amusement at the avatar's responses to what is happening to them.

We want the player to feel surprise and wonder by the depth of how different systems in the game interact.

We want the player to feel tension about choosing to risk the possible negative outcomes of trying out an unidentified item.

Over multiple runs, we want the player to feel a sense of increased mastery in how to handle different situations and growing confidence in their ability to succeed."

We loved the experience of playing Nethack and other traditional roguelikes: the tension of difficult choices and risk-reward equations, the feeling of learning from your mistakes, and the humour and chaos that can happen when small mistakes/bad dice rolls cascade upon each other. Our game systems often surprise *us* and that feels great as a developer and as a player.

The core principle of our game is that mechanics should all interplay with each other in as many ways as possible, as this results in a multiplicative possibility space that has the capacity to surprise even veteran players. The game is punishing, but we hope the humour of the avatar responding to what is being inflicted upon it helps to relieve that, while also providing tangible feedback and gameplay information.
pieces.episodeTitle: The Secret Design in Deep Games
pieces.cardBlurb: I didn't understand this at all at first but then realized how deep it ran, and I was hooked.

pieces.title: Sneaky - The Game
pieces.observation: Sneaky uses stealth mechanics, but I found myself learning specific patterns of enemy movement rather than experimenting with different approaches to avoid being spotted. The guards follow rigid paths, and there seems to be only one correct way through each small level.
pieces.intention: Trivial made Sneaky to explore how minimalist art and shadow could drive gameplay. The aesthetic of light and shadow naturally suggested stealth, but the real design centers on dread and stress: the shock of sudden gunfire, the structural turning point of triggering an alarm, and the cathartic escape as the alarm fades. The dev wanted players to feel the tension of execution under pressure.
pieces.hint: the one where you memorize guard patterns to sneak past

quiz.q: Why did the developer pick an art style of light, shadow and simple shapes?
quiz.right: So they didn't have to really do art
quiz.from: The art style used plays on light and shadows with simple shapes, which allowed me to not have to actually do art (which I'm bad at).

quiz.q: What turns on the red alarm?
wrong: Getting caught for the first time
quiz.from: When the player kills the golden enemy, turning on the red alarm. This is a highlight of the game.

quiz.q: How does the game end?
quiz.right: Out in a calm, well-lit exterior as the alarm fades
quiz.from: When you get out in the well-lit and calm exterior, with the alarm sound getting lower and lower, calming and satisfying end.

answers: I wanted the player to feel a sense of dread and stress. The sudden turn of situation when the alarm starts aimed to be a surprising and exciting turn around upon which the feeling should rather be one of excitement and adrenaline.

The art style used plays on light and shadows with simple shapes, which allowed me to not have to actually do art (which I'm bad at). This in turn pushed me toward the stealth based experience seen in the final game.

The three key moments, I feel, are the following
- when the player gets caught for the first time and gets shot, in a surprisingly powerful and violent sound and visual effects. This has seemed to consistently instill fear and stress into the player.
 - when the player kills the golden enemy, turning on the red alarm. This is a highlight of the game and keeps the experience interesting and progressing, changing the feeling etc...
- when you get out in the well-lit and calm exterior, with the alarm sound getting lower and lower, calming and satisfying end.
 
I also want to point out : this was the first (and only) game I ever completed. Nowaday, most of my design free time is spent in Level Design, making maps for existing game, rather than proper Game Design. Still, although it is small, I still consider this game to be a good and well thought out experience which I'm proud of.

pieces.title: Manboobs The Mini Game
pieces.observation: What makes a space feel like a museum worth exploring versus a set of tasks to complete? Manboobs begins by inviting you to simply look around a strange restaurant filled with absurd references and hidden details, and that freedom feels genuinely fun. But the moment the game gives you a goal—find the portal, reach the next level—that same space becomes a frustrating obstacle course. This was the first game I found, literally, myself, in.
pieces.intention: The developer made this game as an act of creative defiance after leaving AAA work. They wanted players to feel the confusion and freedom they themselves crave: freedom from rigid systems, freedom to interact with everything without purpose. The core idea is a toybox where physics jiggles, models react, and nothing needs justification. They built it around exploration as its own reward, where touching things and watching them move is the entire point, not a means to an end.
pieces.hint: the one where you can just look around the restaurant at the start

quiz.q: Besides confusion, what did the developer want you to feel?
quiz.from: I wanted the player to feel confused, the way in which I am confused with life.. but also extreme freedom, freedom I wish I had in the real world.

quiz.q: What did the developer quit to make this game?
quiz.from: Quitting the bureaucracy of AAA industry to make something truly free and creative.

quiz.q: What's the design rule?
quiz.right: The more jiggles, movement and freedom, the better
quiz.from: As much interaction with everything as possible. The more jiggles, movements, freedom - the better.

answers: I wanted the player to feel confused, the way in which I am confused with life..  but also extreme freedom, freedom I wish I had in the real world.

Quitting the bureaucracy of AAA industry to make something truly free and creative. Doing so in a manic ADHD midlife crisis induced desperation.  Knowing at least I tried something different before crawling back as a failure to the mainstream..
As much interaction with everything as possible.  The more jiggles, movements, freedom - the better
pieces.episodeTitle: The Hidden Reason Bad Game Designs Are Genius
pieces.cardBlurb: Weirdly enough I feel like I understood what the dev was going for...

pieces.title: Zenomatrix
pieces.observation: What if the thing chasing you in a horror game could also be the solution to your puzzle? Zenomatrix asks you to strategically position yourself in danger, looking at and away from mannequins to move them out of your path like living puzzle pieces. It's a unique blending of a classic horror mechanic and a sokoban. Does this merge of opposite genres create something new, or does one always win out over the other?
pieces.intention: Purple Moth built Zenomatrix around a design hypothesis: can horror and puzzles be seamlessly married by making the thing you fear into the thing you must control? The weeping angel mechanic, where statues only move when unwatched, became the core puzzle element. The developer wanted players to start scared, then gradually gain understanding and control as they solve levels, until the game reintroduces genuine horror through new mechanics. This is an intentional design experiment in balancing two genres that work against each other by nature.
pieces.hint: the one where you have to keep the mannequin from seeing you

quiz.q: What is Zenomatrix trying to marry?
quiz.from: ZENOMATRIX is a game design experiment, to see if it was possible to marry the two into a more seamless experience.

quiz.q: What kind of monster is at the heart of it?
quiz.right: A Weeping Angel kind: it moves when you're not looking
wrong: A monster that hunts by sound
quiz.from: I've always been a fan of the "Weeping Angel" mechanic in horror games, those monsters that only move if you're not looking at them.

quiz.q: Which world is just the tutorial?
quiz.from: Be sure to complete the Purple world as that's just the tutorial, the "real game" begins immediately after that.

answers:
-This is a game design experiment of sorts, I'll include the full context in the next section.

-Controls are included in the ""Message Terminal"" window, don't forget to scroll down.

-The game is split into colored ""Worlds"" divided by dark levels, be sure to complete the Purple world as that's just the tutorial, the ""real game"" begins immediately after that.

-This is a puzzle game, if you get stuck, just remember what the game already taught you and experiment with what you can do in the level.

-I hope you enjoy.

I want the player to start out scared, then gradually learn to take control of things as they play more and more levels, and the fear is replaced with understanding...until the game throws them another curve-ball of course.

I grew up playing puzzle games, these are games wracking your brain until you get that Eureka moment is the main attraction, but puzzles do appear in other genres as well, like horror, and I'll be honest, I don't like the way they're used, even in AAA games like the Resident Evil series, or more AA stuff like Poppy Playtime, it feels borderline disrespectful.

It's usually some variation of: ""Get chased by a monster"" then ""do some arbitrary puzzle that barely connects to anything else"" then repeat Ad nauseam.

I do understand why this is the case though, horror and puzzles are opposites by design.

Horror relies on keeping the player in the dark, both thematically and literally, but also mechanically, as well as keeping the player powerless, you're usually in a dimly lit, unfamiliar place, not knowing if you're alone or not,  or whether you have enough bullets (assuming you even get a gun) to fight whatever is lurking in the dark, after all, a horror game immediately looses it's scare factor once you know how everything works, or you have enough control over the situation.

Puzzles on the other hand, are the exact opposite, by design, they are required to communicate all the information the player could possibly need, in order for them to be solvable.

""Here's where you are, here's the exit, here's how everything works and how to manipulate it, good luck.""

This is why, puzzles are usually relegated to either being time fillers between chase sequences, or as a distraction that you have to do WHILE being chased by a monster.
Either way, there's always this wall that separates the two.

ZENOMATRIX is a game design experiment, to see if it was possible to marry the two into a more seamless experience.

To paraphrase the game's, very pretentious, Steam description:
""What if the WILLING acquisition and relinquishment of information (and control), was both the main puzzle mechanic, AND the main horror element?

What if the monster was both a threat to be overcome, but also a puzzle to be solved?""


But how would that work?
Well, the general idea is to take something that can be a source of fear in a horror game, then turn that into a resources you have to manage in order to solve puzzles.

I've always been a fan of the ""Weeping Angel"" mechanic in horror games, those monsters that only move if you're not looking at them (usually a statue or mannequin of some kind, something that isn't supposed to be able to move), games like SCP: Containment Breach made it popular with the SCP-173 monster, and now AAA games like Resident Evil: Shadows Of Rose and even Minecraft with it's new monster ""The Creaking"" have started implementing this type of behavior.

I always thought this kind of enemy had a lot of potential, as it created interesting situations for the player to navigate, and the fact the player had limited control over it made it even more interesting, I thought it was the perfect way to test this little design hypothesis, by making a puzzle game, where this horror monster, is the main mechanic.
pieces.episodeTitle: Can You Design Horror Games Without Fear?
pieces.cardBlurb: Mixing out-of-control with pure control. I felt the dev's intentions exactly.

pieces.title: ESiON
pieces.observation: Why does a game built to convey quiet horror and existential unease feel relaxing instead? ESiON presents a stark, oppressive megastructure where you fish for strange mutated creatures to help your companion with a cryptic ritual, yet the actual moment-to-moment experience of catching fish, selling them, and upgrading your gear feels more like a casual pastime than something unsettling. The tension seems to exist in the world's atmosphere rather than in what you actually do within it.
pieces.intention: The developer wanted to create quiet horror through atmosphere: a harsh contrast between light and dark, cryptic dialogue that leaves players lost, and a massive environment that dwarfs the player alongside two lonely companions. As a person drawn to unsettling moods for comfort, they built ESiON to convey that not all important feelings are positive ones, and that unease can be as valuable as relief.
pieces.hint: the one where the fishing never feels tense

quiz.q: What kind of horror was the developer going for?
quiz.from: This is why I intended to make this style of an atmospheric horror game, I specifically wanted to go for a "quiet horror" vibe.

quiz.q: What's the main game loop?
quiz.from: ...more relaxed as the player understand the main game-loop of fishing and selling fish.

quiz.q: Why is the corridor bigger than the player?
quiz.right: To make you feel small in a big world
wrong: It was a bug they kept
quiz.from: Size comparison, I wanted to convey a sense of scaleness making the player feel smaller than the environment.

answers: I really want to convey the feeling of unsettling atmospheric horror. A sense of scaleness of the big environment compared to the player, as well as a feeling of void or emptiness with only a sense of small hope when seeing your only two companions. After a couple of fishing strikes I want it to still feel tense but at the same time more relaxed as the player understand the main game-loop of fishing and selling fish. This almost morphs into expectation of what the next fish is going to look like or a sense of curiosity into what it is that they're trying to find.

I would describe myself as a more anxious type than the average person. However I do not necessary see it as a hindrance but instead I find comfort in these unsettling moods. Simply put, it feels to me that the rainy days are as important as the sunny days. This is why I intended to make this style of an atmospheric horror game, I specifically wanted to go for a "quiet horror" vibe.

"I would say I focused more on the ""game-feel"" for example a striking sound combined with red indicator on the fishing-rod string to make it feel like the player is catching something and it's a more anxiety inducing sound rather than a fun splash.

The lightning as well, only one point of light and it being a rather harsh contrast between the light and dark. 

Cryptic dialogue was also intended to be felt as a sense of lostness, that the player doesn't quite understand the world and that they have to rely on their own interpretations.

Size comparison, I wanted to convey a sense of scaleness making the player feel smaller than the environment. Mainly the reason why the corridor is bigger that the player and their companions.

From my point of view I feel that I have achieved the feeling that I intended by using the above mentioned ""instruments"""
pieces.episodeTitle: This Game Design Can Drive Players Away
pieces.cardBlurb: Dev wanted megalophobia, though I got relaxation.

pieces.title: Near The Fear
pieces.observation: Near the Fear traps you in a high-speed chase across a highway in an Outrun-styled Hell, pursued by an inexorable shadow. I found myself genuinely dreading capture, feeling real stakes in every moment—but discovered something unexpected: the game offers you a choice between two ways to survive, each with hidden consequences that reshape the world around you in ways the game never explicitly explains.
pieces.intention: The developer built this game as a mirror for internal struggle: the racing mechanics embody anxiety and self-doubt, while the shadow represents pressure that only grows if you avoid it. They wanted players to experience how choices made under stress have rippling consequences—using quick fixes (dark abilities) provides immediate relief but makes things worse; confronting challenges directly (light abilities) is harder now but easier later. The track itself changes based on these choices, turning the world balance mechanic into a interactive lesson about avoidance versus confrontation.
pieces.hint: the one where your choices change the track itself

quiz.q: What does the shadow chasing you stand for?
quiz.from: Shadow chasing you is a portrayal of anxiety, pressure of time and your performance.

quiz.q: What happens to the world when you use Dark abilities?
quiz.right: It turns darker and more chaotic, with more hazards
quiz.from: Using Dark abilities the world is getting more negative, dark, chaotic. This changes visuals, music, but most importantly the track generation itself.

quiz.q: What did the shadow replace from early versions?
quiz.from: In early versions of the game there was only time limit. But I realized time limit is the same as a moving object, and that is much more impactful than a number counter.

answers:
"Player should feel pressured, fighting for survival against all odds, but also rewarded when he/she finally makes progress. I wanted to convey the feeling of something feeling impossible at first, but also encourage the player to continue trying and to believe that if he/she will be doing at least little steps forward and be consistent, he/she can overcome any challenge.
I also wanted to give player a choice how to deal with the dangerous/stressful situations, and a way to see its consequence. That's where abilities come into play. Light abilities require more effort (collecting energy on track) and are quite limited. Dark abilities are on the other hand ""free"" (no energy cost) and can be used often. But there is a short term gain/long term loss trade-off. Using Light abilities the ""world view"" (called World Balance in game) is changing to more positive, light, harmonious. Using Dark abilities the world is getting more negative, dark, chaotic. This changes visuals, music, but most importantly the track generation itself (number of hazards on track, hazards, if barriers are present, ...)."

I think (nearly) every person has this internal struggle (that he/she is not enough, is afraid of something, has any kind of anxiety etc.) and I'm no exception. I wanted to portray this feeling in a game, because I believe games have this unique power to express (and explore) complex themes with interactivity and immersion. So basically solving an analogue problem in a magic circle, a simulation, with rules, mechanics and tools to help player learn a way to solve it in reality too. I wanted to help others with their internal struggle and give them a tool to conquer it.

The random generation of the track should convey the uncertainty, and create discomfort of not knowing what comes next. Shadow chasing you is a portrayal of anxiety, pressure of time and your performance. In early versions of the game there was only time limit. But I realized time limit is the same as a moving object, and that is much more impactful than a number counter.
The idea of a racing/driving game with roguelite elements excited me as a great metaphor for internal battle. Failing a lot at first and then getting better, feeling the progress with every run. There are more layers of progression. Temporary, permanent, and unlocking new abilities. Temporary upgrades should create variety in each run, motivating the player to try it "one more time". I feel it isn't there yet, but I want to create more creative and fun modifiers/upgrades to increase this aspect. Permanent upgrades should feel as a greater reward for longer term effort. And unlocking new abilities should feel like like the biggest reward.
The World Balance mechanic - a world view/perspective shifting as a consequence of your actions is conveying an idea that when you're always avoiding the problems, they tend to only grow bigger. And vice versa - that confronting them is harder in short term, but you make it easier for yourself in the long run.
pieces.episodeTitle: Why Some Games Never Stay With You
pieces.cardBlurb: I loved every part of this horror racer. But I completely missed the metaphor of anxiety.

pieces.title: Polariball
pieces.observation: Polariball borrows from pinball and arcade classics, but something about its casual pacing and random obstacles feels directionless compared to the permanent fixtures and clear goals of those games. I found myself most engaged not chasing targets, but in moments of clear focus like the snake mode—suggesting the game's real appeal might lie somewhere other than where its design seems to be pointing.
pieces.intention: Zion D. Hill built Polariball around the pinball fantasy: high-energy arcade flow, quick sessions, and the hypnotic pull of 'just one more game.' The developer meticulously crafted responsive audio, non-stop motion, and skill-building through repeated play to create that almost meditative state. Oddly enough, the arcade flow was inspired by both Crazy Taxi and Tetris. Neat.
pieces.hint: the one with magnets that pull a ball toward random targets

quiz.q: What should players say to themselves at the game over screen?
quiz.from: The big moment I was aiming for is when looking at the game over screen you tell yourself "Just one more game...".

quiz.q: Which arcade game's producer does the developer quote?
quiz.from: "...the whole point of the game (Crazy Taxi) is to have a lot of fun in a short period of time" - Kenji Kanno.

quiz.q: Besides Crazy Taxi, what is the developer a huge fan of?
quiz.from: I am also by extension a huge fan of pinball and wanted to construct an experience that gives me the same sense of flow and growth.

answers:
"From the very beginning, I really wanted to make an experience that makes players say to themselves ""Just one more game..."".
In support of this goal, it was really important to me that the game induces a flow state through its gameplay and presentation. 
I hope that players feel a sense of satisfaction through growing their skills and beating their (or their friends) high scores!"

"“…the whole point of the game (Crazy Taxi) is to have a lot of fun in a short period of time, and it’s a very concentrated game.” - Kenji Kanno (producer of Crazy Taxi)

Most of my favorite games are high energy arcade experiences (like Crazy Taxi) that let me just get into the game and have fun with it. The lack of friction given to the player to simply boot up a game and play a few quick rounds is an experience that I really want to see more of. 
I am also by extension a huge fan of pinball and wanted to construct an experience that gives me the same sense of flow and growth that I get from honing my skills on a specific table.
These desires as a player were the fuel to the fire of this game's development, and they also helped me form a very clear goal for the player experience early on because I already knew what fans of similar games would be looking for in a game like this."

"As I mentioned before, the big moment I was aiming for is when looking at the game over screen you tell yourself ""Just one more game..."". 
I tried to make sure the game length was quick and snappy to support this. This moment naturally came up a lot for players when playtesting, so I definitely feel that I was able to achieve this experience.
Inducing a flowstate in the same way games like Tetris or Pinball do was also very important to me. The audio in the game was very meticulously designed by my team to try and pull you in the zone as you play, with the music being responsive to the moment-to-moment gameplay. 
The game mechanically reflects this goal by having a sense of motion that feels very non-stop. Even in the slower gameplay moments the player needs to maintain their focus and control of the ball in order to do well.
My hope is that these two factors combine to have an almost hypnotic effect to the player where they can just sit back and tune-in on the game for a bit."
pieces.episodeTitle: Everyone Loves This Game. What Am I Missing?
pieces.cardBlurb: I found a relaxing skill-based focusing game, though the dev wanted addictive arcade fun.

pieces.title: Depth Complaint
pieces.observation: Why is this eclectic world of broken assets and self deprecating humor such a fun game? Depth Complaint layers RPG Maker's familiar systems with jarring aesthetics and jokes that only work when you actively engage with them—a victory certificate that kills you, a legendary sword protected by sheep, and my favorite meta-meta-joke: a regular treasure chest that offers a potion. But beneath the comedy and the developer's visible exhaustion, something stranger happens: the literally unfinished game becomes whole through theming and metaphor.
pieces.intention: The developer made Depth Complaint as a learning project that weaponized its own incompleteness. They wanted players to feel the discomfort of exploring something released midway through development—using collage, placeholder assets, physical sketches, and deliberate lack of balance to blur the line between unfinished and intentional. By embracing the unfinished state as a conceptual choice rather than a failure, they could release the game whenever learning felt complete.
pieces.hint: the one that wasn't finished

quiz.q: What feeling is Depth Complaint going for above all?
quiz.right: That the game isn't finished and something's off
quiz.from: The number one thing I'm going for is a sense that the game isn't finished, and that there's something just off about it.

quiz.q: What does the developer love working with?
quiz.from: I really enjoy working with collage, whether visual or sound.

quiz.q: What are the battle sprites made from?
quiz.from: ...and the use of physical sketches for battle sprites contribute to the themes of the game.

answers:
"The number one thing I'm going for is a sense that the game isn't finished, and that there's something just off about it.  Deliberate lack of balance, somewhat player-hostile design, and disorienting visuals, text, and sound.  Blurring the lines between placeholder assets and intention.

I wanted it to feel like the player was exploring something released midway through development."

I really enjoy working with collage, whether visual or sound.  I wanted to just make something to learn the ropes of the engine and game dev in general, and decided to make that intention part of the game itself.  Having it "unfinished" became a deliberate choice very early in development, and meant I could simply release it once I felt like I had learned enough.

"I think the inclusion of references to outside material, the transparent use of almost entirely square tiles that don't directly represent any real objects, and the use of physical sketches for battle sprites contribute to the themes of the game.

If I could change anything, I would've not used any of the default RPGMaker assets until later in the game."
pieces.episodeTitle: Art Doesn't Need To Be Finished
pieces.cardBlurb: An unfinished game, by definition and by design. Completely my type of game.

pieces.title: Cyber Volley
pieces.observation: Cyber Volley presents you with a character chasing a dream despite real hardship, entering a sports competition, and facing rivals—but you discover there's no way to fail, no score too low, and no reason the world around you seems to care how well you do. The question becomes: what is this game actually asking you to care about?
pieces.intention: Helixstar built Cyber Volley as a technical study in character-controller and physics interaction rather than as a designed player experience. The developer chose a platforming twist they could execute with limited programming skills: a character controller with a ball physics body. They wanted to create accessible, simple controls and light-hearted character dialogue wrapped around a difficult personal story, hoping these elements would inspire players to move forward.
pieces.hint: the one where you enter a volley tournament

quiz.q: What is Cyber Volley's twist on platforming?
quiz.right: You bounce a ball off your head
quiz.from: Just make a character controller, a ball with a rigid body, and put a trigger on the player's head that adds force to the rigidbody.

quiz.q: Why was it made?
quiz.right: As a technical study for a first solo project
quiz.from: This is my first solo project. Programming is not my expertise... It was made as a technical study.

quiz.q: Why are the obstacles easy to understand?
quiz.right: So you spend your thinking on the ball, not the puzzle
wrong: Because there was no time for more
quiz.from: I created obstacles that are easily understood, so people spend more mental energy on positioning the ball correctly instead of figuring out "the puzzle".

answers: I wanted the players to feel engaged with the character and the ball's movement. I wanted players to feel rewarded both by their reflexes and their strategy in positioning the ball. Also, I wanted to make characters with a lot of personality in the game's world.

This is my first solo project. Programming is not my expertise. So I came up with a platformer mechanic twist that I never seen before, and that I could apply with my coding skills. Just make a character controller, a ball with a rigid body, and put a trigger on the player's head that adds force to the rigidbody. It was made as a technical study. Also, I love platformers, and I like to work with non-conventional mehcanics. Also, I wanted to make non-intrusive, optional plot points through dialogue.

I made the controls as simple as I could, since no extra buttons are required for regular bumps on the ball. I tried to create light-hearted character dialogue, and also show a difficult part of the protagonist's life, so as to inspire the players to move on despite life's challenges. I created obstacles that are easily understood, so people spend more mental energy on positioning the ball correctly instead of figuring out "the puzzle".
pieces.episodeTitle: The Biggest Problem in Game Design Isn't Design
pieces.cardBlurb: I was look for stakes in this game and didn't find any. But what the dev intended.

pieces.title: Acrobatic Car
pieces.observation: Why would a game designed to evoke the organic obsession of early-2000s flash games need to teach you its advanced techniques in the tutorial levels? Acrobatic Car demands mastery from the start, showing you how to exploit its physics to fly and perform acrobatic maneuvers before you've even chosen to care about doing so. The question is whether demanding obsession from a player can ever create the same magic as obsession that grows naturally from play.
pieces.intention: The developer made Acrobatic Car out of love for Elasto Mania and similar flash games that've disappeared. They wanted to recapture that era's sense of nostalgia and simplicity, while adding modern mechanics and ideas. They designed the game around iterations of mechanics tuned to deliver dopamine rushes from completing hard tracks and a sense of novelty in the game's movement systems.
pieces.hint: the one where you need to be obsessed to play

quiz.q: Which game era should it make you nostalgic for?
quiz.from: Nostalgic (make them remember the old fun days of flash games era).

quiz.q: Which classic did the developer play as a kid?
quiz.from: I was having fun in my childhood playing the classic game Elasto Mania and many other monster trucks flash games.

quiz.q: What can you make yourself in it?
quiz.right: Your own tracks, in a level editor
wrong: Your own cars, part by part
quiz.from: ...I want them to feel creative making their own tracks via built-in level editor.

answers:
"-Nostalgic (make them remember the old fun days of flash games era)
-Simplicity (make them feel that they play the game, not the game playing them by demanding grinding and consuming their time to understand so complex systems)
-Challenge (make them get a dopamine rush upon beating a hard track)
-Neophilia (make them feel they have played a really new game, new mechanics, new experience, and not the same familiar game formulas repeating over and over like nowadays) 
-Creative (like old days when games were having level editors to unleash player's creativity and imagination, I want them to feel creative making their own tracks via built-in level editor)"

I was having fun in my childhood playing the classic game Elasto Mania and many other monster trucks flash games, and suddenly these kinds of games that I loved had suddenly disappeared for various reasons, so I always waited for this genre of games to show up again. waited any developer to make a similar game but that didn't happen. so, I decided to make one by myself and add modern mechanics and ideas to it.
It's all about iterations, dozens of ideas and mechanics that I kept adding and removing and tweaking through the early development process.
pieces.episodeTitle: Games Can't Force You To Love Them
pieces.cardBlurb: This felt like it was made for the obsessed flash-game kid. I'm not that person.

pieces.title: Credit Farm/Debtician
pieces.observation: Why does buying a hammer with a credit card feel so strange, even when the mechanical systems that reward you for it work perfectly well? Credit Farm presents a deck-building game about racking up debt through wild spending, but the objects you purchase—construction supplies, beach balls, trophies—seem disconnected from any reason you'd actually buy them. The game's synergies and number systems create genuine strategic satisfaction, yet something about the world refuses to make sense.
pieces.intention: Shroombot built Credit Farm around the pure pleasure of deck-building synergy and the fantasy of spending without limits. They wanted players to strategize with credit cards and feel the dopamine hit of discovering how different items combine.
pieces.hint: the one where you use credit cards to buy construction supplies

quiz.q: How many coins should players scrape together after feeling like they'd lose?
quiz.from: ...then manage to find a bunch of nice items that makes them get to 3 coins.

quiz.q: What should you have fun doing before a level starts?
quiz.from: Also, before starting the level, they should have fun trying to come up with nice card synergies.

quiz.q: Why are there no tutorial levels?
quiz.right: Locking you to a few items would ruin the fun
quiz.from: I find that teaching the player a certain mechanic by locking them down to only a couple of items would ruin the fun.

answers: I wanted the player to feel like they're losing and that they won't manage to pull though in a level, then manage to find a bunch of nice items that makes them get to 3 coins. Also, before starting the level, they should have fun trying to come up with nice card synergies.

I chose this experience because I wanted the player to feel the fun of strategizing and planning ahead, but also the feeling of being able to buy anything you want and trying to squeeze as much profit as possible from a level.

First of all, there isn't a clear path to victory. This makes it harder since you can't exactly plan how to finish a level most optimally, but it's fun to test out the build you already made and see what items you get. The lack of "tutorial levels" also hints to this, since I find that teaching the player a certain mechanic by locking them down to only a couple of items would ruin the fun.
pieces.episodeTitle: When Games Forget How Reality Works
pieces.cardBlurb: I got a strangely surreal experience from buying things in this game. Dev didn't intend that.

pieces.title: Enemies Within
pieces.observation: Why does a game about confronting trauma feel funny? Enemies Within begins with lighthearted humor and cartoonish visuals, then suddenly asks you to feel the weight of death, darkness, and despair—but the tonal shifts happen so quickly that the serious moments land as dark comedy instead of drama.
pieces.intention: The developer built Enemies Within around specific emotional arcs: safety in the opening town, mounting dread in the cave, a climactic struggle with a boss, and then a descent into unease before recovery. Each section is meant to embody different forms of inner turmoil—despair, anxiety, grief—and to explore how we help others through their own struggles while carrying our own.
pieces.hint: the one where the characters are two stick figures

quiz.q: What should the player feel they've gone through by the end of the loop?
quiz.from: By the end of the established game loop, I want the player to feel like they have gone through the process of confronting and overcoming trauma.

quiz.q: What does the game lean on in boss fights instead of timing dodges like Dark Souls?
quiz.from: Unlike games like Dark Souls which have more emphasis on timing dodges to avoid attacks, I am designing boss fights and levels around fully utilizing the player's movement capabilities.

quiz.q: What happens after a boss fight?
quiz.right: You lose abilities and go slower for a while
quiz.from: ...lose abilities and be forced to navigate a section of the game in a slower and more methodical manner.

answers: By the end of the established game loop, I want the player to feel like they have gone through the process of confronting and overcoming trauma. To achieve this, I am hoping the player feels safe and curious in the first town and slowly strip away from the feeling of safety as they explore the cave. I want the cave boss fight to be the climax which provides a struggle the player must overcome to progress. Although I want the player to be able to relax a little after the boss fight, I also want the player to feel a sense of unease throughout the entire next section. I hope that this sense of unease will then be lifted in the hub area where the player unlocks a new ability and regains the abilities that were lost.

My intent is to showcase the processing of various kinds of inner turmoil, including the processing of second-hand turmoil that comes from helping others processing their own turmoil. I hope to build levels and boss fights around inner turmoil such as despair, anxiety, and grief. I am excited for this experience because I want to tell the story that I feel like a lot of people are feeling at this time in a way that is entertaining. I feel like a lot of people struggle with mental health, and that there are a lot of people out there preying on people with these struggles. I feel like we often decouple mental health issues from those in power attempting to take advantage of people who are struggling, so I hope to cleanly connect these concepts as the game progresses. When I started this game, I was intending on making a simple platformer, but the story is largely what is pushing me forward.

"From a mechanics perspective, I want the player to generally feel empowered through freedom of movement. Unlike games like Dark Souls which have more emphasis on timing dodges to avoid attacks, I am designing boss fights and levels around fully utilizing the player's movement capabilities to gain the upper hand against enemies.
In general, I am hoping to achieve the above feelings by the following game loop: (1) start off in a safe area, (2) explore a level and fight a boss that each embodies a specific inner turmoil, (3) lose abilities and be forced to navigate a section of the game in a slower and more methodical manner, and (5) return to a safe area to unlock new abilities."

pieces.title: Ominoflux
pieces.observation: Ominoflux presents itself as a Tetris-like puzzle game where you stack falling blocks and eliminate rows, but I discovered that this intuitive strategy actually works against the game's design. Only after learning the developer's intended approach—focusing on collecting gems to upgrade stats rather than clearing lines—did the game's systems suddenly click into place, transforming from frustrating to engaging,
pieces.intention: The developer built Ominoflux around achieving a flow state through mastery of layered, interconnected systems. They wanted players to experience a game that feels hectic and difficult at first, then becomes genuinely fun once understood—where clearing lines is mere survival and gem collection and stat optimization are the true path to victory. The flux mechanic, spawning blocks, gem timing, and combat are designed to work together cohesively, but the game was developed in isolation. The developer prioritized creating something genre-pushing and unique as opposed to another Tetris clone.
pieces.hint: the one where you have to prioritize gems over clearing lines

quiz.q: Which game did the developer first play co-op with family?
quiz.from: Tetris was the very first game I ever played co-op with family. So I went after this.

quiz.q: Which of these was one of their rules?
quiz.from: 1 - To avoid any genre that is trending (vampire survivor like, slot like, etc.)

quiz.q: In Ominoflux, clearing lines is...
quiz.from: Again, clearing lines is merely surviving the onslaught. You cannot count on just clearing lines in this game.

answers:
Similar to Tetris, I am hoping the player could enter a certain ""flow state"". 

I want the player to feel that the game is hectic, difficult and nuanced at first, but once mastered becomes really fun - even easy!

I want the player to feel pride in mastering the layered mechanics, and be able to show off skills and perform clutch plays.

For the game, I set out a number of non-negotiable things:

1 - To avoid any genre that is trending (vampire survivor like, slot like, etc.)
2 - To avoid any genre that is over saturated (platformer, horror, etc.)
3 - To avoid anything that required heavy graphics (visual novels, RPGs, etc.)
4 - I preferred 2D over 3D, at least for now.
5 - The game MUST be unique. If a game out there already existed with my planned idea - I would go back to the drawing board.

That eliminated a lot. List basically came down to either puzzle games, or some kind of space exploration game... just a handful of limited options.

Tetris was the very first game I ever played co-op with family. So I went after this. 

Did a lot of research into similar block falling games including:

Lumines, Dr. Mario, Capcom Puzzle Fighter, Drop Dutchy, Facetris, Welltris, Puyo Puyo, etc.

I was always amazed at how basic Tetris is, yet it had deep strategic play, and is such a classic. I felt that this genre could do with another title that pushed the limits. Maybe merged with another genre or something. I felt like I just had to try!

I am not really sure to be honest. The game is deep with several layered mechanics. I think if a player manages to master everything then yes... I may just succeed in getting the player to feel all-powerful, in a game that most people can hardly master?

Game mechanics-wise: It is meant to be relentless, and mistakes compound quickly. It is certainly not a cozy puzzle game. 

Clearing lines is just survival. The key is really in optimizing how you place the gems in order to win faster. 

Story mode - gems are the key to levelling up faster to beat the whole campaign long term.

Hi-Score mode - gems are the key to increase score multipliers.

PVP - gems are the key yo defeating the opponent.

Again, clearing lines is merely surviving the onslaught. You cannot count on just clearing lines in this game.

New lines of blocks spawn inevitably. Thus you are always down-stacking. This isn't like Tetris where you can do triple or quad clears easily... this is survival line by line, as you try to grapple with gems and other systems.

pieces.title: Tangled Crisis
pieces.observation: Tangled Crisis presents an intriguing contradiction: it deliberately hides a maze you must navigate from view, and encourages memory skills. pieces.intention: Long Sleeve Games built Tangled Crisis around a specific idea: what if you could see a complete maze, but the moment you started moving, your vision collapsed into a small circle around you? The developer wanted to explore how limiting information changes the experience of maze navigation, focusing on reflex skills and memory in combination. The vision mechanic itself is the central design experiment, evolved organically from that initial constraint.

pieces.title: Monster Freaks!
pieces.observation: Monster Freaks presents itself with fast-paced music, a vengeance narrative, and combat-heavy scenarios, yet the actual path to victory seems to be finding an exit rather than clearing enemies. pieces.title: Spring Escape Deep Down
pieces.observation: Why does a game about discovering a vast world feel confined? Spring Escape Deep Down evokes the exploratory joy of classic platformers like Sonic and Earthworm Jim, with beautifully charming pixel art. Yet the giant explorative world feels small to me because the levels feel compartmentalized, presenting isolated challenges one after another rather than inviting a more flowy experience. The hub world hints at something larger, but the structured levels don't quite deliver that same sense of uncovering a living world.
pieces.intention: ELE designed Spring Escape Deep Down around the feeling of being a small creature discovering a much larger world piece by piece. The environments were deliberately scaled to dwarf the player character, with careful details meant to reward exploration and discovery. Each mechanic and obstacle was built as part of a cohesive living world rather than random challenges. The game wants to be simple and accessible, a quiet adventure of slow revelation where you learn about this world at the same pace as your character does.
pieces.hint: the one where you play as a tiny flower root exploring a huge world

quiz.q: What should you feel like you're doing?
quiz.from: I wanted the player to feel like slowly uncovering a world in a simple, easy to pick up and play adventure.

quiz.q: What does the game NOT want to be?
quiz.right: A high challenge or an epic adventure
quiz.from: You're not here for a high challenge or an epic adventure, the game wants to be simple but really well done.

quiz.q: How are many locations built compared to the player?
quiz.from: ...not only are many locations way bigger in scale than the player character but there is plenty of care on environmental details.

answers:
I wanted the player to feel like slowly uncovering a world in a simple, easy to pick up and play adventure. Many times you'll be in awe at finding out a big environment or set-piece, other times you'll rush through obstacles and other times you'll meet new mysterious characters that may or may not aid you.
Often times you're alone, but the world around you just feels richer and richer.

This game in many aspect is my first "real" game, the first commercial one, the one to really introduce a bigger scope and ongoing narrative, and with that I wanted to create an experience of slowly discovering little bits of a small part of a much bigger world through the perspective of a character that knows just as much as you do about it. You're not here for a high challenge or an epic adventure, the game wants to be simple but really well done.

The environments were especially built around the idea of being a new creature uncovering a giant world, not only are many locations way bigger in scale than the player character but there is plenty of care on environmental details and variety that give you that sense of discovery and pushing forward.
A lot of the game's mechanics, obstacle wise, tend to be built around this feeling of a cohesive world, you're not just interacting with random elements but with real living parts of this world.

pieces.title: Warlord's Penance
pieces.observation: I'm stupid. After playing this incredibly hard dungeon crawler, I discovered I had spent most of my playthrough fighting the game's systems rather than mastering them, accidentally making the game much more difficult than it needed to be. The game feels like an action title but demands the methodical, transactional thinking of a strategy game. If you're privy to this kind of thinking, goody for you. It didn't work for me.
pieces.intention: The developers built Warlords Penance around combat that feels accessible but requires players to think strategically rather than reactively. They wanted to create a approachable dungeon crawler that avoids the complexity, grinding, and wiki-dependency of classic games in the genre. Each mechanic—the cooldown system, partial damage from regular blocks, adaptive difficulty—was designed to create pressure and engagement while remaining fair.
pieces.hint: the one where blocking still damages you slightly

quiz.q: What should you feel after every enemy encounter?
quiz.from: I want the player to feel a slight relief after every enemy encounter they overcome.

quiz.q: What does the developer find too hard to approach in classic dungeon crawlers?
quiz.right: Stats, complexity, grind and needing a wiki
quiz.from: I love the idea of classic dungeon crawlers, but I think they're too difficult to approach/enjoy (stats, complexity, grindy, need wiki, etc).

quiz.q: Whose adaptive difficulty did they point to?

answers: I want the player to feel constantly pressured, while feeling engaged with the continuous progress (unlocked doors, getting a new ally, getting close to the exit). I want the player to feel a slight relief after every enemy encounter they overcome. We're trying to make it so the game is not unfair, but far from being an "easy" walk in the park.

"I wanted to try a simple yet engaging combat system.
Plus, I love the idea of classic dungeon crawlers, but I think they're too difficult to approach/enjoy (stats, complexity, grindy, need wiki, etc). Also I love old school dark fantasy setting (which once again is reserved to few games that are not easily approachable).
We wanted to make a game that is simple to make, simple to play, and could be expanded all while still being approachable. :)"

- What's next? For the extended commercial release we're planning to add more content (dungeons levels), equipment, such as better swords, shields, bows, and a simple skilltree. These wouldn't be super complex, just to provide a more streamlined sense of progress. Let me know your thoughts

pieces.title: Diecast
pieces.observation: Balatro but dice? Diecast looks like a deck-builder at first glance, with its shop, modifiers, and multipliers arranged just like Balatro. But every time you roll, you're starting from scratch. I found myself drawn to the scoring categories on screen rather than the point totals they were actually trying to reach, and couldn't quite internalize all the small modifiers that determined whether a roll was good or wasted.
pieces.intention: Sofamire made Diecast as a version of Yahtzee designed to be fun to play repeatedly. The core idea is that players should feel dopamine hits from big numbers and from discovering overpowered builds. Unlike a traditional deck-builder where probability converges as you modify your deck, Diecast resets probability with each roll, asking players to build strategy around dice that have fixed but specific behaviors (odd-only, Fibonacci sequences, copied values) and score categories they can buy and upgrade.
pieces.hint: the one where you build dice like a deck builder

quiz.from: I wanted to make a version of Yahtzee that was fun to play and a surprise every time.

quiz.q: Who did they make Diecast for first?

quiz.q: Where do the dopamine hits come from?
quiz.right: Big numbers and finding an overpowered build

answers: I wanted the player to feel engaged and excited about building different strategies as they go through a run, having a build they’re going for, but also the excitement of changing a build on the fly. I wanted the player to feel there’s a possibility that their build isn’t good enough and may not get them through to the end.

Diecast is a game I made for myself first, because I wanted to make a version of Yahtzee that was fun to play and a surprise every time. It supposed to be an engaging solitaire-style experience with added depth. It’s like a mechanical puzzle, finding which dice, items, and score work together, and then deeper than that finding ways to game the system (make extra money, sell off scores that won’t be used for early cash flow, etc., waiting to end a level to get a few more hands in (leveling them up further in the process).
Dopamine hits from big numbers, but also from finding an overpowered build.

pieces.title: Hope Timbre
pieces.observation: Hope Timbre is a beautiful representation of metaphorical gameplay. It asks you to collect instruments from dreams and bring them into reality, but the connection between my actions and their effects remained mysteriously distant to me. You play through beautiful puzzle levels, return to a hub world, and notice the world has grown slightly warmer. It's easy to miss that you're responsible for this change.
pieces.intention: Peter built Hope Timbre from watching his own son's experience with music therapy and sound-based treatment. He wanted players to feel a 'wow effect' with each puzzle level and—crucially—to feel empathy for two siblings trying to heal their world. The core mechanic of gathering items from dreams to use in reality embodies his belief that even in imagination, there is hope and strength to change things. He adapted the rotation mechanic from observing insects moving through foliage, making the player's movement itself feel natural and alive.

quiz.from: As the game is about collecting instruments and songs in dreams and using them to heal a broken world of two little siblings...

quiz.q: What inspired the main mechanic of rotating around flower icons?
quiz.right: Watching an insect climb through leaves

answers: I wanted the player to feel the wow effect when playing each level - each is different in terms of puzzles, decorations and music. We use adaptive music in a way that each time a part of puzzle is solved, music changes a little and at the end of each stage the music is evolved to the maximum. As the game is about collecting instruments and songs in dreams and using them to heal a broken world of two little siblings, I wanted players to feel empathy for the little ones and the urge to help them. Also, listen to some cute songs you collect and see the children happy about it, while each instrument also heals the world overall. I wanted to see players see the change the music offers.

My son is ill with several diagnosis, he needs physiotherapy among other things. Music was always a very entertaining and soothing thing for him. He also attends to a music - therapy and a special Tomatis therapy that uses sound to rewire the brain, leading to improved motor skills, cognition, communication, and emotions.

I got the idea for main mechanic (rotating on flower icons to open new path) when I was observing how insect travels through the foliage - as long as it sticks to it, there is no gravity involved so it can rotate and climb anywhere. I restricted this to specific points only. The mechanic to gather items in dreams and use them in the world where children live -  I wanted the player to realize that even in dreams and music, you can find hope and strength to change things.
