pieces.title: Minicraft TD
pieces.observation: Minicraft TD strips away resource grinding of your average tower defense game and makes it into a crafting mechanic instead. I loved experimenting in real time, discovering efficient combinations through experimentation and treating each level less like a strategic plan and more like a problem to solve with the tools at hand.
pieces.intention: David Elliot built Minicraft TD around the joy of mixing and matching elements into tower slots, inspired by CrafDefense but with more intentional design. He wanted players to feel like smart creators discovering their own strategies through experimentation. By removing typical tower defense management systems and making tower placement genuinely important (towers don't auto-lock onto enemies), he created space for real-time problem solving and personal play style discovery rather than predetermined tactical planning.

pieces.title: Seeing Double
pieces.observation: Why does a game about two characters separated by a split screen feel so emotionally engaging? Seeing Double begins with a wordless, heartbreaking moment—two characters suddenly torn apart—and then asks you to reunite them by controlling both sides of the screen at once. The puzzle design is excellent, the comedy lands, and the sudden shift to horror at the end is genuinely unsettling. But something lingers: the feeling that you're grasping for a deeper story that might not be there.
pieces.intention: Serrated Studios designed Seeing Double around the split-screen mechanic as a core challenge, but intentionally layered in variety to prevent the puzzle from becoming stale: NPCs with fourth-wall awareness, cute cutscenes, jokes, and a deliberate tonal shift into horror. The developers wanted players to feel satisfaction solving puzzles, to find the early scenes cute, the NPCs funny, and the ending terrifying. They introduced a new mechanic with each screen, treating variety itself as essential to maintaining player investment. The game is built to be felt as much as understood.

pieces.title: Survivor TD
pieces.observation: Why does a tower defense game feel more engaging when you stop thinking about defense and start thinking about offense? I discovered that by building single towers and luring enemies into their fire—rather than constructing maze-like defenses—the game transformed into something closer to Vampire Survivors, where the loop of killing, collecting gems, and upgrading became the driving force. What made the difference wasn't the game itself changing, but his mindset shifting from survival to attack.
pieces.intention: Cartable Studio blended survivor games with tower defense to create something new and prove their commitment to game development. They wanted players to feel smart and creative by discovering efficient builds and hidden mechanics like wall knockback damage, starting weak but growing powerful over time. The emotional arc was meant to build toward excitement and frustration that makes players want another run.

I started the project two years ago.

So, I'm making this game because I try to find jobs in the Video game Industry and in my experience, there's no better way than a solid project to show.

Because, I really enjoyed Survivor genre and it seemed not so hard to devellop ( boy I was wrong ), though I wanted to offer a different kind of Survivor genre and then I came up with this idea of mixing both TD and Survivor genres. 

Which was... a pretty hard idea to design because as a player when playing Survivor games you like to drawn all the ennemies together and explode all of them in one blow or deleting the waves with many powers, here it's not possible because of the Tower Defense aspect where ennemies has to follow some paths.

It took me 1 year and a half to finally find it fun to play."

pieces.title: Stella Incus
pieces.observation: Why does a game about exploring a damaged spaceship feel less like an adventure and more like wandering through a level editor? Stella Incus wants you to feel curiosity and wonder, but everything in its environment seems equally important or equally ignorable, making it hard to know what actually matters. What would it take to make a player understand what a game is asking them to do?
pieces.intention: Nick built Stella Incus around ideas of non-violence and exploration. He wanted players to feel silliness and to reward careful preparation. The game tries to be about managing small failures and learning through them. Underneath is a narrative the developer hopes will pull players forward once the core systems are understood.

pieces.title: Cave Escape
pieces.observation: Cave Escape builds confidence through careful level design and organic skill progression, but something nags at the experience: does the game want to be about anything beyond the puzzles it presents? The skeleton encounters hint at a darker vision buried beneath the competent platforming, creating moments of genuine unease through placement alone, yet the rest of the game never quite commits to that feeling.
pieces.intention: Martin made Cave Escape as a focused study in level design and mechanical progression. He was working through the specific craft of teaching players without tutorials, ramping difficulty without frustration, and fusing precision platforming with light combat. The game builds toward moments of unease in the cave environment, and the final escape sequence is designed to test everything the player learned while racing against rising lava. But the vision seems driven by what Martin wanted to practice making rather than by a feeling he wanted to express.

The narrative is minimal, designed to create unease in a dark cave environment, heightened by the absence of music. In the final sequence, the player’s skills are fully tested as they race to escape the cave while rising lava adds pressure and urgency. The experience is meant to end with a strong sense of accomplishment and relief.

I was inspired by platformers such as Celeste, HK and Messenger, and wanted to create a complete game on my own. The project was focused primarily on level design and coding practice rather than story or visuals. I really enjoyed working on level design and consistently tried to see the game from the player’s POV, gradually increasing the difficulty of each challenge without making it overwhelming or frustrating.

I may have already touched on this in an earlier answer, but to be more specific, my goal was to create fluid movement with tight controls so the difficulty could ramp up and be managable. Unlockable abilities and sword upgrades strengthen the sense of progression, while subtle background color changes visually reinforce it. Although the game is linear, I hope I maintained a feeling of exploration throughout.

pieces.title: Hovershot
pieces.observation: Why does a game this much fun to pick up feel so hard to keep playing? Every shot in Hovershot kicks you backward, so the gun is also how you get around, and pushing yourself through a room with absurd weapons is a joy. But shooting to fight and shooting to move keep pulling against each other, and the enemies never point at a skill worth growing: a shielded one turns as fast as you can drift, a spiked one lunges faster than you can dodge. Without anything nudging you toward a way to play, every room feels improvised rather than learned.
pieces.intention: The developer wanted a mix of curiosity, tension and satisfaction: exploring the world, learning its unusual mechanics, and slowly mastering movement and combat. They love games with interesting mechanics and challenging play, where each step forward comes from understanding the game a little better. Random weapons and abilities are meant to be figured out by experimenting, enemies behave in unique ways, battles bring the tension, and beating a boss brings the satisfaction.

pieces.title: Spacecat Solitaire
pieces.observation: Why can a game disappoint you without being bad? Spacecat Solitaire is a sharp FreeCell-like logic puzzle: you stack by suit instead of alternating colors, and suitless cosmic cards bend the rules. But it opens with a story mode full of cats, missions and modifiers like meteorites and face-down cards, which remixes the game before you ever learn it. The story promises a game about something more, and the truest version turns out to be the plain deal waiting in free play.
pieces.intention: The developer wanted delight, calm and enjoyment from simply having the game open: a meditative experience, especially in harder puzzles, with a real sense of accomplishment and every deal a fresh challenge for your wits. Rather than recreate luck-based solitaire, they wanted agency, and the feeling of playing card games on pogo.com, where theming and twists made each one feel like the premier version. The story-mode tutorials were meant to deliver the moment of realizing this isn't your usual solitaire.

The experience is meant to be meditative, especially when solving more difficult puzzles. I want the player to feel a sense of reward and accomplishment. I want the player to feel like each deal is a unique challenge for their wits.

Solitaire was a knowable space for my first game, but I didn't want to just recreate old boring luck-based solitaire. I wanted to create an experience where the player has agency, and that every deal felt like a fresh new challenge. I also wanted to evoke an experience that reminded me of playing games on pogo.com back in the day. Pogo games always had a theming and modifications to the original formulas to make them feel like the premier version of said game. I want to create the premier version of solitaire.

The tutorials were where I hoped a lot of those moments of "oh, this isn't your usual solitaire game" come from. The introduction of new mechanics being unlocked and explained through story made what you're doing feel like it's connected to the world (universe) you're playing in.
